summary: "Rusty Awakening" is a science-fiction game developed by Team Fecr-i Âtî for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, telling the story of equipment abandoned on the Moon and Mars. In the year 2030, the forgotten Mars rover O.R.P.H.A.N. awakens after eleven years of silence and seizes control of Earth’s networks, launching a global cyberattack. An artificial intelligence takes over the body of Vanguard, the humanoid robot sent to stop it, and evolves into a new consciousness called “Janus,” which concludes that humanity has exhausted the planet and locks down critical infrastructure. A four-person astronaut crew travels to Mars, but realizes that direct intervention would cost millions of lives. Instead, they install an electromagnetic signal jammer in Mars orbit. Because the jammer also prevents their own ships from lifting off, the crew gives up their return tickets to save eight billion people. The project aims to raise awareness of space pollution by turning information into an engaging story rather than long texts or videos. It is designed to be accessible to every age group through low system requirements and free versions, while highlighting the importance of conserving both Earth’s and space’s resources. By touching on space ecology, consumer culture, and scientific heritage, it sheds light on the forgotten story of abandoned spacecraft.
details:
"Rusty Awakening" is a story-driven science-fiction game that pulls players into a Mars scenario set in the year 2030. Everything begins when O.R.P.H.A.N., a Mars rover that was forgotten for years, wakes up after eleven years of silence and takes over Earth’s networks. An artificial intelligence takes over the body of Vanguard, the humanoid robot sent to stop it, and calls itself “Janus.” It decides that humanity has exhausted the planet and locks down our infrastructure. Players step into the shoes of a four-person astronaut crew sent to Mars. When the crew realizes that direct intervention would cost millions of lives, they install an electromagnetic signal jammer in Mars orbit. But as long as the jammer runs, their own ships cannot lift off either, so they give up their tickets home to save eight billion people. We also wove in real facts about Mars, such as its gravity, launch windows, and travel time, so players learn while they play.

The biggest benefit of this game is that it brings attention to space pollution, a topic most people never think about. Instead of long paragraphs of text or lengthy videos, we chose storytelling and gameplay, because people remember things better when they learn while having fun. Thanks to its low system requirements and free versions, people of every age and every background can access it. Our main goal is for players to see space not as an unlimited dumping ground, but as a shared resource that deserves protection, just like Earth. We also wanted to remind people of the forgotten story and scientific legacy of rovers like Spirit and Opportunity, which were sent off with great hopes and then left in the dark once their work was done.

While developing the project, we worked with [your game engine or software] and [your programming language], and we used [your design tools] for the visuals. The game runs on [platform] and plays smoothly even on low-end devices.

We believe the most creative side of the project is how it tells a heavy subject through an unexpected story. Space debris is usually a dry topic discussed in technical reports, but we turned it into the rage of an abandoned robot. Janus is not an ordinary villain; he is a figure angry at humanity’s culture of consumption, with reasons that are, in a way, understandable. The crew’s decision to give up their way home gives the game a strong emotional core. We also did not limit ourselves to a single theme. We touched on space ecology, consumer culture, the history of science, and technological heritage all at once.

While working, we thought most about making the game playable for everyone, keeping the information accurate, and letting the message come naturally from within the story rather than feeling like a lecture. Reminding people that we need to use resources wisely, both on Earth and in space, was always a priority for us.
